Hand axe: earliest widespread use 1.7 Mya (Africa). A hand axe (or handaxe or  Acheulean hand axe) is a prehistoric stone tool with two faces that is the longest-used tool in human history.

Adze: earliest widespread use c. 8000 BC (Worldwide). An adze () or adz is an ancient and versatile cutting tool similar to an axe but with the cutting edge perpendicular to the handle rather than parallel.

Felling axe: earliest widespread use c. 8000 BC (Eurasia). An axe (; sometimes spelled ax in American English; see spelling differences) is an implement that has been used for thousands of years to shape, split, and cut wood, to harvest timber, and as a weapon.
Broad axe: earliest widespread use c. 1000 BC (Europe). A broadaxe is a large broad-headed axe.

Hatchet: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A hatchet (from the Old French hachete, a diminutive form of hache, 'axe' of Germanic origin) is a single-handed striking tool with a sharp blade on one side used to cut and split wood, and a hammerhead on the other side.
Claw hammer: earliest widespread use c. 1st c. AD (Rome). A claw hammer is a hammer primarily used in carpentry for driving nails into or pulling them from wood.
Sledgehammer: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Europe). A sledgehammer or sledge is a tool with a flat, massive, often metal head, attached to a long wooden or solid handle.

Mallet: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A mallet is a tool used for imparting force on another object, often made of rubber or sometimes wood, that is smaller than a maul or beetle, and usually has a relatively large head.
Maul: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Europe). A maul may refer to any number of large hammers, including:
Splitting wedge: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A wedge is a triangular shaped tool, a portable inclined plane, and one of the six simple machines.
Chisel: earliest widespread use c. 6000 BC (Worldwide). A chisel is a hand tool with a characteristic wedge-shaped cutting edge on the end of its blade.
Gouge: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Eurasia). Gouge may refer to:
Centre punch: earliest widespread use Iron Age (Eurasia). A punch is a tool used to indent or create a hole through a hard surface.
Awl: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). Awl may refer to:
Bradawl: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A bradawl is a woodworking hand tool with a blade similar to that of a straight screwdriver and a handle typically made from wood or plastic.
Handsaw: earliest widespread use c. 2000 BC (Egypt). In woodworking and carpentry, hand saws, also known as "panel saws", are used to cut pieces of wood into different shapes.

Frame saw: earliest widespread use Roman (Rome). A frame saw or sash saw is a type of saw which consists of a relatively narrow and flexible blade held under tension within a (generally wooden) rectangular frame (also called a sash or gate).

Bow saw: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A bucksaw is a metal-framed crosscut saw in the shape of a bow with a coarse wide blade generally used with a sawbuck to cut logs or firewood to length (bucking).
Two-man crosscut saw: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A crosscut saw (thwart saw) is any saw designed for cutting wood perpendicular to (across) the wood grain.
Hacksaw: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A hacksaw is a fine-toothed saw, originally and mainly made for cutting metal.
Coping saw: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A coping saw is a type of bow saw used to cut intricate external shapes and interior cut-outs in woodworking or carpentry.

Tenon saw: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A backsaw is any hand saw which has a stiffening rib on the edge opposite the cutting edge, enabling better control and more precise cutting than with other types of saws.
Wooden jack plane: earliest widespread use Roman (Rome). A hand plane is a tool for shaping wood using muscle power to force the cutting iron (blade) over the wood surface.

Spokeshave: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A spokeshave is a hand tool used to shape and smooth woods in woodworking jobs such as making cart wheel spokes, chair legs, paddles, bows, and arrows.
Drawknife: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A drawknife (drawing knife, draw shave, shaving knife) is a traditional woodworking hand tool used to shape wood by removing shavings.
Froe: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A froe (or frow), shake axe or paling knife is a tool for splitting wood by cleaving it along the grain.

Bow drill: earliest widespread use c. 10000 BC (Worldwide). A bow drill is a simple hand-operated type of tool, consisting of a rod (the spindle or drill shaft) that is set in rapid rotary motion by means of a cord wrapped around it, kept taut by a bow which is pushed back and forth with one hand.
Brace and bit: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A brace is a hand tool used with a bit (drill bit or auger) to drill holes, usually in wood.
Auger: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). An auger is a device to drill wood or other materials, consisting of a rotating metal shaft with a blade at the end that scrapes or cuts the wood.
Gimlet: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A gimlet is a hand tool for drilling small holes, mainly in wood, without splitting.
Hand drill: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A hand drill is the simplest primitive method to produce rapid rotary motion of a rod.
File: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Eurasia). A file is a tool used to remove fine amounts of material from a workpiece.
Rasp: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A rasp is a coarse form of file used for shaping wood, metal, or other material.
Whetstone: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). Whetstone may refer to:
Grindstone: earliest widespread use Roman (Worldwide). A grindstone, also known as grinding stone, is a sharpening stone used for grinding or sharpening ferrous tools, used since ancient times.
Smith's tongs: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Eurasia). Tongs are a type of tool used to grip and lift objects, often too hot to hold, instead of holding them with the hands.

Anvil: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Eurasia). An anvil is a metalworking tool consisting of a large block of metal (usually forged or cast steel), with a flattened top surface, upon which another object is struck (or "worked").

Swage block: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A swage block (or swager block) is a large, heavy block of cast iron or steel used in smithing, with variously sized holes in its face and usually with forms on the sides.
Bellows: earliest widespread use c. 1500 BC (Eurasia). Bellows are a device constructed to expel a controlled blast of air.
Bench vise: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A vise or vice (British English) is a mechanical apparatus used to secure an object to allow work to be performed on it.
Pliers: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Eurasia). Pliers are a hand tool used to hold objects firmly, possibly developed from tongs used to handle hot metal in Bronze Age Europe.
Pincers: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Eurasia). Pincer may refer to:

Monkey wrench: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). An adjustable spanner (UK), also called a shifting spanner or shifter (Australia and New Zealand) or adjustable wrench (US and Canada), is any of various styles of spanner (wrench) with a movable jaw, allowing it to be used with different sizes of fastener head (nut, bolt, etc.) rather than just one
Screwdriver: earliest widespread use 1400s (Europe). A  screwdriver is a tool, manual or powered, used for turning screws.

Crowbar: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A crowbar is a lever consisting of a metal bar with a single curved end and flattened points, used to force two objects apart or gain mechanical advantage in lifting; often the curved end has a notch for removing nails.
Pickaxe: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A pickaxe (American spelling: pickax), pick-axe, or pick is a generally T-shaped hand tool used for digging.
Mattock: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A mattock () is a hand tool used for digging, prying, and chopping.

Rock hammer: earliest widespread use 1800s (Worldwide). A geologist's hammer, also known as rock hammer, rock pick, geological pick, or geo pick, is a specialized hammer used for splitting and breaking rocks.
Davy lamp: earliest widespread use 1815 (Britain). The Davy lamp is a safety lamp used in flammable atmospheres, invented in 1815 by Sir Humphry Davy.

Hand-steel drill (jack hammer): earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A jackhammer (pneumatic drill, breaker, demolition hammer or road hammer in Commonwealth English) is a pneumatic or electro-mechanical tool that combines a hammer directly with a chisel.
Shovel: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A shovel is a tool used for digging, lifting, and moving bulk materials, such as soil, coal, gravel, snow, sand, or ore.

Spade: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Europe). A spade is a tool primarily for digging, consisting of a long handle and blade, typically with the blade narrower and flatter than the common shovel.
Garden trowel: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A trowel is a small hand tool used for digging, applying, smoothing, or moving small amounts of viscous or particulate material.
Hoe: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A hoe is an ancient and versatile agricultural and horticultural hand tool used to shape soil, remove weeds, clear soil, and harvest root crops.

Rake: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A rake (Old English raca, cognate with Dutch hark, German Rechen or Harke, from the root meaning 'to scrape together', 'heap up') is a broom for outside use; a versatile horticultural implement consisting of a toothed bar fixed transversely to a handle, or tines fixed to a handle, and used to collec
Pitchfork: earliest widespread use Iron Age (Eurasia). A pitchfork or hay fork is an agricultural tool used to pitch loose material, such as hay, straw, manure, or leaves.
Hay fork: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). Hayfork may refer to:
Scythe: earliest widespread use Iron Age (Europe). A scythe (, ) is an agricultural hand-tool for mowing grass or harvesting crops.

Sickle: earliest widespread use c. 10000 BC (Levant). A sickle, bagging hook, reaping-hook or grasshook is a single-handed agricultural tool designed with variously curved blades and typically used for harvesting or reaping grain crops, or cutting succulent forage chiefly for feeding livestock.

Billhook: earliest widespread use Iron Age (Europe). A billhook or bill hook is a versatile cutting tool used widely in agriculture and forestry for cutting woody material such as shrubs, small trees and branches.
Machete: earliest widespread use 1500s (Americas). A machete (; Spanish pronunciation: [maˈtʃete]) is a broad blade originating from Central America.
Secateurs: earliest widespread use 1800s (France). Pruning shears, also called hand pruners (in American English) or secateurs (in British English), are a type of scissors used for plants.
Sheep shears: earliest widespread use Iron Age (Eurasia). Shears may refer to:

Hedge shears: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A hedge trimmer, shrub trimmer, or bush trimmer is a gardening tool or machine used for trimming (cutting, pruning) hedges or solitary shrubs (bushes).

Wheelbarrow: earliest widespread use c. 100 AD (China). A wheelbarrow is a small hand-propelled load-bearing vehicle, usually with just one wheel, designed to be pushed and guided by a single person using two handles at the rear.
Ard plough: earliest widespread use c. 4000 BC (Mesopotamia). The ard, ard plough, or scratch plough is a simple light plough without a mouldboard.
Moldboard plough: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A plough or plow (US) (both pronounced ) is a farm tool for loosening or turning soil before sowing seed or planting.
Harrow: earliest widespread use Roman (Eurasia). In agriculture, a harrow is a farm implement used for surface tillage.

Seed drill: earliest widespread use 1701 (England). A seed drill is a device used in agriculture that sows seeds for crops by positioning them in the soil and burying them to a specific depth while being dragged by a tractor.
Threshing flail: earliest widespread use Medieval (Eurasia). Flail may refer to:
Winnowing basket: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). Winnowing is a process by which chaff is separated from grain.
Saddle quern: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A quern-stone is a stone tool for hand-grinding a wide variety of materials, especially for various types of grains.
Millstone: earliest widespread use Roman (Worldwide). Millstones or mill stones are stones used in gristmills, used for triturating, crushing or, more specifically, grinding wheat or other grains.

Mortar and pestle: earliest widespread use c. 35000 BC (Worldwide). A mortar and pestle is a set of two simple tools used to prepare ingredients or substances by crushing and grinding them into a fine paste or powder in the kitchen, laboratory, and pharmacy.

Ox yoke: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A yoke is a wooden beam used between a pair of oxen or other animals to enable them to pull together on a load when working in pairs, as oxen usually do.
Milk pail: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). Pail may refer to:

Cheese press: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A cheese press is a device for pressing whey from curds when making cheese.
Cheese mould: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). Cheesemaking (or caseiculture) is the art of making cheese.
Milking stool: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A stool is a raised seat commonly supported by three or four legs, but with neither armrests nor a backrest.
Bee skep: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A beehive is an enclosed structure in which honey bees raise their young and produce honey as part of their seasonal cycle.
Bee smoker: earliest widespread use 1873 (USA). A bee smoker (usually called simply a smoker or a smokepot) is a device used in beekeeping to calm honey bees.
Honey extractor: earliest widespread use 1865 (Austria). A honey extractor is a mechanical device used in extraction of honey from honeycombs.

Fishing rod: earliest widespread use c. 2000 BC (Egypt). A fishing rod  or fishing pole is a long, thin rod used by anglers to catch fish by manipulating a line ending in a hook (formerly known as an angle, hence the term "angling").

Fish hook: earliest widespread use c. 40000 BC (Worldwide). A fish hook or fishhook, formerly also called an angle (from Old English angol and Proto-Germanic *angulaz), is a hook used to catch fish either by piercing and embedding onto the inside of the fish mouth (angling) or, more rarely, by impaling and snagging the external fish body.
Fishing net: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). A fishing net or fish net is a net used for fishing.
Fish trap: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A fish trap is a trap used for catching fish and other aquatic animals of value.

Fishing harpoon: earliest widespread use c. 90000 BC (Africa). A harpoon is a long, spear-like projectile used in fishing, whaling, sealing, and other hunting to shoot, kill, and capture large fish such as sharks or marine mammals such as seals, sea cows, and whales.
Lobster pot: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A lobster trap or lobster pot is a portable trap that traps lobsters or crayfish and is used in lobster fishing.
Snare trap: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). Animal trapping, or simply trapping or ginning, is the use of a device to remotely catch and often kill an animal.
Tape measure: earliest widespread use 1829 (Britain). A tape measure or measuring tape is a long, flexible ruler used to measure length or distance.

Ruler: earliest widespread use c. 2500 BC (Indus). A ruler is an instrument used to make length measurements, whereby a length is read from a series of markings called "rules" along an edge of the device.

Set square: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A set square or triangle (American English) is an object used in engineering and technical drawing, with the aim of providing a straightedge at a right angle or other particular planar angle to a baseline.
Try square: earliest widespread use Ancient (Egypt). A square is a tool used for marking and referencing a 90° angle, though mitre squares are used for 45° angles.

Plumb bob: earliest widespread use c. 2500 BC (Egypt). A plumb bob, plumb bob level, or plummet, is a weight, usually with a pointed tip on the bottom, suspended from a string and used as a vertical direction as a reference line, or plumb-line.

Spirit level: earliest widespread use 1661 (France). A spirit level, bubble level, or simply a level, is an instrument designed to indicate whether a surface is horizontal (level) or vertical (plumb).

Chalk line: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A chalk line or chalk box is a tool for marking long, straight lines on relatively flat surfaces, much further than is practical by hand or with a straightedge.

Dividers: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). Calipers or callipers are an instrument used to measure the linear dimensions of an object or hole; namely, the length, width, thickness, diameter or depth of an object or hole.

Sundial: earliest widespread use c. 1500 BC (Egypt). A sundial is a horological device that tells the time of day (referred to as civil time in modern usage) when direct sunlight shines by the apparent position of the Sun in the sky.
Hourglass: earliest widespread use c. 1300 (Europe). An hourglass (or sandglass, sand timer, or sand clock) is a device used to measure the passage of time.
Water clock: earliest widespread use c. 1500 BC (Egypt). Clepsydra may refer to:  Clepsydra, an alternative name for a water clock.
Balance scale: earliest widespread use c. 2400 BC (Indus). A scale or balance is a device used to measure weight or mass.
Steelyard balance: earliest widespread use Roman (Rome). A steelyard balance, steelyard, or stilyard is a straight-beam balance with arms of unequal length.
Spring scale: earliest widespread use 1770 (Britain). A spring scale, also known as a spring balance or newton meter, is a type of mechanical force gauge or weighing scale.
Magnetic compass: earliest widespread use c. 200 BC (China). A compass is a device that shows the cardinal directions used for navigation and geographic orientation.

Astrolabe: earliest widespread use c. 200 BC (Greece). An astrolabe (Ancient Greek: ἀστρολάβος, romanized: astrolábos, lit. 'star-taker'; Arabic: ٱلأَسْطُرلاب, romanized: al-Asṭurlāb; Persian: ستاره‌یاب, romanized: Setāreyāb) is an astronomical instrument dating to ancient times.
Sextant: earliest widespread use 1731 (Britain). A sextant is a doubly reflecting navigation instrument that measures the angular distance between two visible objects.
Mercury thermometer: earliest widespread use 1714 (Germany). A thermometer is a device that measures temperature (the hotness or coldness of an object).
Barometer: earliest widespread use 1643 (Italy). A barometer is a scientific instrument that is used to measure air pressure.
Drop spindle: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A spindle is a straight spike, usually made from wood, used for spinning, twisting fibers such as wool, flax, hemp, and cotton into yarn.
Distaff: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A distaff (, , also called a rock) is a tool used in spinning.
Spinning wheel: earliest widespread use c. 1000 (India). A spinning wheel is a device for spinning thread or yarn from fibres.
Wool comb: earliest widespread use Iron Age (Europe). Combing is a method for preparing carded fibre for spinning.

Hand cards: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). In textile production, carding is a mechanical process that disentangles, cleans and intermixes fibres to produce a continuous web or sliver suitable for subsequent processing.
Niddy-noddy: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A niddy-noddy is a tool used to make skeins from yarn.

Warp-weighted loom: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Europe). The warp-weighted loom is a simple and ancient form of loom in which the warp yarns hang freely from a bar, which is supported by upright poles which can be placed at a convenient slant against a wall.
Backstrap loom: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Americas). A loom is a device used to weave cloth and tapestry.
Weaving shuttle: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A shuttle is a tool designed to neatly and compactly store a holder that carries the thread of the weft yarn while weaving with a loom.
Flying shuttle: earliest widespread use 1733 (England). The flying shuttle or fly shuttle is a type of weaving shuttle.

Spinning jenny: earliest widespread use 1764 (England). The spinning jenny is a multi-spindle spinning frame, and was one of the key developments in the industrialisation of textile manufacturing during the early Industrial Revolution.

Sewing needle: earliest widespread use c. 50000 BC (Siberia). A sewing needle, used for hand-sewing, is a long slender tool with a pointed tip at one end and a hole (or eye) to hold the sewing thread.
Bone needle: earliest widespread use c. 50000 BC (Worldwide). Needle or Needles may refer to:
Thimble: earliest widespread use Roman (Rome). A thimble is a small pitted cup worn on the finger that protects it from being pricked or poked by a needle while sewing.
Sewing machine: earliest widespread use 1790 (England). A sewing machine is a machine used to sew fabric and materials together with thread.

Scissors: earliest widespread use c. 1500 BC (Egypt). Scissors or shears are hand-operated cutting tools that consist of a pair of pivoting blades whose sharpened edges slide firmly against and past each other when the handles (shank) on the opposite side of the pivot are squeezed shut.
Knitting needles: earliest widespread use c. 1000 (Egypt). A knitting needle or knitting pin is a tool in hand-knitting to produce knitted fabrics.
Crochet hook: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A crochet hook is a tool used to create loops in thread or yarn and to interlock them into crochet stitches.
Embroidery hoop: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). Embroidery hoops and frames are tools used to keep fabric taut while working embroidery or other forms of needlework.
Tatting shuttle: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). Tatting is a technique for handcrafting a particularly durable lace from a series of knots and loops.

Sad iron: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A clothes iron, also known as a flatiron, smoothing iron, dry iron, steam iron, and simply iron, is a small appliance that, when heated, is used to press clothes to remove wrinkles and unwanted creases.

Dye vat: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). Dyeing is the application of dyes or pigments on textile materials such as fibers, yarns, and fabrics with the goal of achieving color with desired color fastness.

Fulling stocks: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). Fleshing beam: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). Tanning, or hide tanning, is the process of treating skins and hides of animals to produce leather.
Cobbler's last: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A last is a mechanical form used by shoemakers and cordwainers in the manufacture and repair of shoes.
Skinning knife: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). The skinner knife or skinning knife is a professional tool for a skinner.
Hide scraper: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). In prehistoric archaeology, scrapers are unifacial tools thought to have been used for hideworking and woodworking.
Flint blade: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). In archaeology, a lithic blade is a type of stone tool created during lithic reduction by striking a long narrow flake from a stone core.

Stone knife: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). A knife (pl.: knives; from Old Norse knifr 'knife, dirk') is a tool or weapon with a cutting edge or blade, usually attached to a handle or hilt.
Fire drill: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). A fire drill is a method of practicing how a building should evacuate in the event of a fire or other emergencies.
Fire plough: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Oceania). A fire plough (or fire plow) is a firelighting tool.

Flint and steel: earliest widespread use Iron Age (Eurasia). A fire striker or fire steel is a tool used in fire making, consisting of a piece of steel that can be struck against a flint, chert, or other hard rock in order to generate sparks.

Tinderbox: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A tinderbox, or patch box, is a container made of wood or metal containing flint, firesteel, and tinder (typically charcloth, but possibly a small quantity of dry, finely divided fibrous matter such as hemp), used together to help kindle a fire.
Friction match: earliest widespread use 1826 (England). A match is a tool for starting a fire.

Pocket lighter: earliest widespread use 1823 (Germany). A lighter is a portable device which uses mechanical or electrical means to create a controlled flame, and can be used to ignite a variety of flammable items, such as cigarettes,  butane gas, fireworks, candles, or campfires.

Tinder bracket: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Europe). Fomes fomentarius (commonly known as the tinder fungus, false tinder fungus, hoof fungus, tinder conk, tinder polypore or ice man fungus) is a perennial wood-decay basidiomycete found in Europe, Asia, Africa and North America.

Hammerstone: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). In archaeology, a hammerstone is a hard cobble used to strike off lithic flakes from a lump of tool stone during the process of lithic reduction.

Pitching tool: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). Stonemasonry, also called stonework or stonecraft, is the creation of buildings, structures, and sculpture using stone as the primary material.
Brick mould: earliest widespread use c. 3000 BC (Mesopotamia). A brick is a type of building material used to build walls, pavements, and other elements in masonry construction.

Mortar tub: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). Mortar  is a workable paste which hardens to bind building blocks such as stones, bricks, and concrete masonry units, to fill and seal the irregular gaps between them, spread the weight of them evenly, and sometimes to add decorative colours or patterns to masonry walls.

Pulley: earliest widespread use c. 1500 BC (Mesopotamia). A pulley is a wheel on an axle or shaft enabling a taut cable or belt passing over the wheel to move and change direction, or transfer power between itself and a shaft.

Block and tackle: earliest widespread use Roman (Rome). A block and tackle, purchase, or only tackle is a system of two or more pulleys with a rope or cable threaded between them, used to provide tension and lift heavy loads.

Winch: earliest widespread use Ancient (Greece). A winch is a mechanical device that is used to pull in (wind up) or let out (wind out) or otherwise adjust the tension of a rope or wire rope (also called "cable" or "wire cable").
Windlass: earliest widespread use Ancient (Greece). The windlass  is a type of horizontal winch used to move heavy weights, featuring a cylinder (barrel) operated by a crank to wind a rope.

Capstan: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A capstan is a vertical-axled rotating machine developed for use on sailing ships to multiply the pulling force of sailors when hauling ropes, cables, and hawsers.
Lever: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A lever is a simple machine consisting of a beam or rigid rod pivoted at a fixed hinge or fulcrum.
Ladder: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). A ladder is a vertical or inclined set of rungs or steps commonly used for climbing or descending.
Grappling hook: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A grappling hook, or grapnel, is a drag-looking device intended for grappling onto something.

Iron shackle: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A shackle (or shacklebolt), also known as a gyve, is a U-shaped piece of metal secured with a clevis pin or bolt across the opening, or a hinged metal loop secured with a quick-release locking pin mechanism.

Iron chain: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A chain is a serial assembly of connected links typically made of metal, with an overall character similar to that of a rope in that it is flexible and curved in compression, but linear, rigid, and load-bearing in tension.

Padlock: earliest widespread use c. 1000 BC (Eurasia). Padlocks are portable locks with a shackle that may be passed through an opening (such as a chain link, or hasp staple) to prevent use, theft, vandalism or harm.

Door key: earliest widespread use c. 2000 BC (Egypt). Pin tumbler lock: earliest widespread use c. 2000 BC (Egypt). The pin tumbler lock, also known as the Yale lock (after Linus Yale Jr) is a lock mechanism that uses a series of spring-loaded pins of varying lengths to prevent the lock from opening without the correct key.
Lever lock: earliest widespread use 1778 (England). A lever tumbler lock is a type of lock whose mechanism uses a set of levers to prevent the bolt from moving in the lock.
Door hinge: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A hinge is a mechanical bearing that connects two solid objects, typically allowing only a limited angle of rotation between them.

Iron nail: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Worldwide). In woodworking and construction, a nail is a small object made of metal (or wood, called a tree nail or "trunnel") which is used as a fastener, as a peg to hang something, or sometimes as a decoration.
Wood screw: earliest widespread use 1500s (Europe). A screw is an externally helical threaded fastener capable of being tightened or released by a twisting force (torque) to the head.
Nut and bolt: earliest widespread use 1500s (Europe). A bolt is an externally helical threaded fastener capable of being tightened or released by a twisting force (torque) to a matching nut.
Rivet: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Worldwide). A rivet is a semi permanent mechanical fastener.
Glue pot: earliest widespread use Ancient (Egypt). Animal glue is an adhesive that is created by prolonged boiling of animal connective tissue in a process called rendering.

Clamp: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A clamp is a fastening device used to hold or secure objects tightly together to prevent movement or separation through the application of inward pressure.
Sawhorse: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). In woodworking, a saw-horse or sawhorse (saw-buck, trestle, buck) is a trestle structure used to support a board or plank for sawing.
Workbench: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A workbench is a sturdy table at which manual work is done.

Pole lathe: earliest widespread use c. 1300 BC (Egypt). Wood turning gouge: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). Woodturning is the craft of using a wood lathe with hand-held tools to cut a shape that is symmetrical around the axis of rotation.

Cooper's adze: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A cooper is a craftsman who produces wooden casks, barrels, vats, buckets, tubs, troughs, and other similar containers from timber staves that were usually heated or steamed to make them pliable.
Barrel hoop driver: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A barrel or cask is a hollow cylindrical container with a bulging center, longer than it is wide.
Spoked wheel: earliest widespread use c. 2000 BC (Eurasia). A wheel is a rotating component (typically circular in shape) intended to turn on an axle bearing.
